<action type="say">
Let’s quickly figure out how urgent this is and prevent damage.

First, a few questions:
1) Is any pipe or fitting under the sink visibly cracked, bulging, or leaking/dripping right now?
2) Do you still get water from that kitchen faucet (hot or cold), or is it completely stopped?
3) Is this an inside wall sink or on an outside wall (against the exterior of the house), and what’s roughly your outdoor temperature right now?

While you check that, do these right away:
- DO:
  - Turn off the water to that sink if you can find the shutoff valves under it (turn them clockwise to close).
  - If you can’t find them, tell me and I’ll help you locate the main shutoff instead.
  - Open the faucet (hot and cold) to relieve pressure.

- DON’T:
  - Don’t use an open flame (blowtorch, lighter, etc.).
  - Don’t aggressively hit or bend the pipes.
  - Don’t turn the water back on fully if you notice any new leaks.

If you feel comfortable, look under the sink now and tell me:
- What type of pipe it looks like (copper/metal, white plastic, gray plastic)?
- Whether you see frost/ice on the outside of the pipe?

Once I know if there’s any leaking or visible damage, I can tell you if this is “urgent, call a plumber now” vs. “can probably thaw carefully yourself,” and I can walk you step-by-step through what to do (or help you book a plumber if you’d prefer). </action>

<action type="say">
This is time-sensitive but not an emergency yet since there’s no leak. The main risk is when the ice starts to thaw, so we want to control that.

Do this in order:

1) Open things up and relieve pressure
- Open the cabinet doors under the sink so warm room air can get in.
- Turn the kitchen faucet handles all the way ON (both hot and cold) and leave them open.
- For now, leave the shutoff valves under the sink OPEN. We only close them if you see a leak.

2) Start gently warming the pipe
If you have any of these, use one:
- Hair dryer: Best option. Set to low/medium, keep it moving back and forth along the metal pipe, especially the frosty part. Start closer to the faucet and work back toward the wall.
- Heating pad or warm towels: Wrap around the frozen section, re-warm the towels as they cool.
- Small space heater: Point it so it warms the space under the sink (not right up against anything flammable).

Avoid:
- No open flames (torch, lighter, etc.).
- Don’t overheat plastic parts or the P-trap; focus on the metal supply line.

3) Watch carefully for what happens
- Good sign: You’ll start to hear water sputter or trickle from the faucet as the ice melts. Let it run at a small stream for a while once it’s flowing freely.
- Problem sign: If you see ANY dripping, spraying, or water suddenly appearing under the sink or hear water inside the wall where it shouldn’t be:
  - Immediately close the shutoff valves under the sink (turn them clockwise until tight).
  - If the leak doesn’t stop or you can’t reach those, turn off the main water to the house.

4) When this becomes “urgent plumber” territory
- If you can’t get any flow back after ~30–45 minutes of gentle warming, or
- If you see a leak at any point,  
then it’s time to get a plumber involved as soon as possible.

I can:
- Stay with you step-by-step while you do this, or
- Help you find and book a same-day/emergency plumber near you.

Tell me:
1) Do you have a hair dryer or space heater you can safely use right now?
2) Roughly how cold is it outside?
3) Do you want to try thawing it yourself for a bit, or would you rather I help line up a plumber right away (and if so, what city/ZIP are you in)? </action>
